tagline: High mountains and barren plateaus connect fossil quarries and museums
intro: The Dinosaur Diamond loops through western Colorado and eastern Utah, crossing high mountains and barren plateaus between fossil quarries and museums. Colorado DOT highlights the dinosaur collections and the Colorado and Green rivers along this National Scenic Byway, designated in 2002. It lists 486 miles for the two-state loop and suggests two to three days. On the Colorado leg, Highway 139 crosses 8,205-foot Douglas Pass, with a few switchbacks and a seven-percent grade on its south side.

The loop joined roads with separate histories. Near Moab, residents campaigned for a riverbank road to replace the difficult Heavenly Stairway pack trail. King's Toll Road replaced that trail by 1902, improving travel but remaining vulnerable to flooding because it lay too low beside the river. Colorado designated its byway in 1997 and Utah its Prehistoric Highway in 1998, before national recognition joined them in 2002.

Starting west of Fruita, follow I-70 toward Cisco and SR 128 toward Moab, then turn north through Green River, Price and Helper. US 191 climbs toward Duchesne; US 40 continues east through Vernal and Jensen toward Dinosaur. The quarry is a separate excursion north of Jensen. Return through Rangely and over Douglas Pass to Fruita and the interstate.

moments.title: Castle Gate
moments.text: Two sheer sandstone walls frame the Price River near the mouth of Price Canyon, giving Castle Gate its name. The mining town developed after the railroad crossed the Wasatch Plateau; its first mine opened around 1886 and supplied coal for steam trains. When Castle Gate incorporated in 1914, the Utah Fuel Company and the Denver and Rio Grande Western Railroad owned and tightly controlled the town. An explosion at Mine No. 2 killed 172 miners in 1924. The town itself was dismantled in 1974, and residents moved to a subdivision west of Helper. Coal-loading facilities replaced the former townsite beside the railway.

moments.title: Dinosaur Quarry
moments.text: The Wall of Bones holds thousands of fossils in a rock layer tilted 67 degrees from horizontal. Earl Douglass found eight Apatosaurus vertebrae here in 1909 while working for the Carnegie Museum. Rivers had carried the animals into the sediments that became solid rock; mountain building later lifted and tilted those layers, and erosion exposed them. The quarry building needed its own engineering response to the ground: after structural problems forced closure in 2006, the Park Service rebuilt the exhibit hall on steel columns reaching bedrock. The quarry reopened in 2011.

moments.title: Fruita
moments.text: The town sits in the high desert of the Colorado Plateau, with the Colorado River and Book Cliffs among its surrounding features. Dinosaur Hill earned its name through the bones found there, including a Brontosaurus skeleton discovered by Elmer Riggs and his crew in 1901. Riggs worked with a Field Museum crew from Chicago. They recovered nearly two-thirds of that skeleton, and other sauropod bones followed. The animals came from the late Jurassic and lay within the Morrison Formation. Colorado DOT includes the Dinosaur Journey Museum in Fruita among the byway features.
